project.name: InterviewProof AI
project.description: AI-powered interview-prep / career-coaching SaaS built on Next.js 16. Two halves: a customer-facing diagnostic, scoring, and practice flow, and an autonomous internal "Command Center" of company agents (CEO orchestrator, directors, executive assistant) that take guardrailed, spend-capped actions surfaced in an admin dashboard. (Analysis scoped to backend + routes: src/server, src/app, src/lib, src/types and root config; the src/components UI library was excluded.)

tour.title: Project Overview & Entry Point
tour.description: InterviewProof AI is a two-sided Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19) SaaS: one half gives job-seekers AI-driven interview diagnostics and practice, the other runs an autonomous internal "Command Center" of company agents. The root layout is the entry point of the whole App Router tree — it sets global metadata, imports global styles, and wraps every page. Start here to anchor where the runtime begins before branching into the two product halves.

tour.title: Auth Middleware & Deployment Wiring
tour.description: Before any route handler runs, edge middleware refreshes the Supabase auth session so server components and API routes see a logged-in user. The Vercel config registers the scheduled cron jobs that drive the autonomous agent runs you will meet at the end of the tour. Together these two files define the request lifecycle and the deployment surface the rest of the app sits on.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js middleware runs at the edge before the matched route. It can rewrite, redirect, or mutate cookies — here it transparently rotates the Supabase session so downstream handlers never see a stale token.

tour.title: Shared Types & Domain Vocabulary
tour.description: Both product halves speak a common language defined here. The central type catalog declares the project's shared interfaces (reports, scoring, diagnostics), while the company-agent type module defines the autonomous subsystem's roles, actions, and constants. Reading these establishes the vocabulary that recurs in every later step.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript barrel/index modules re-export many declarations from one path. A high fan-in file like this (imported by ~80 other files) is the project's contract layer — change it and the whole codebase feels it.

tour.title: Customer Journey: Creating & Analyzing a Report
tour.description: The customer flow begins when a user submits a resume and job description. The create route persists a new report record, and the analyze route kicks off the full diagnostic pipeline. These handlers are the front door to the scoring engine and show how Next.js route handlers validate input, enforce rate limits, and hand off to server-side intelligence.

tour.title: The Analysis Pipeline, Scoring Engine & RAG
tour.description: This is the brain of the customer product. The pipeline orchestrates the prepare → LLM → complete phases and assembles the diagnostic report. The scoring engine barrel re-exports the deterministic modules (archetype, forecast, HireZone, practice intelligence) that turn raw LLM analysis into structured scores, while the RAG layer retrieves rubric chunks and curated resources to ground the analysis. Building on the report routes from Step 4, this is where the actual diagnostic intelligence is computed.

tour.title: Customer Agents & Shared Context Loader
tour.description: Beyond the one-shot report, users get conversational AI specialists. The shared context loader hydrates an AgentContext from Supabase so every agent sees the same user history. The readiness-coach, mock-interview, and debrief agents each call Claude with that context to coach, simulate interviews, and analyze post-interview performance. The context loader's high fan-in shows how every customer agent depends on this single hydration point.

tour.title: Agent API Routes & PDF Report Delivery
tour.description: The customer agents from Step 6 are exposed through thin API routes — here the mock-interview route creates a session and runs the agent. The report PDF route closes the customer loop by rendering the finished diagnostic as a downloadable document. This shows the consistent pattern: route handler authenticates, creates a session, runs the agent or renderer, returns the result.

tour.title: The Command Center Admin Dashboard
tour.description: Now we cross to the autonomous half. The Command Center page gates on admin auth and fires any due company agents on visit, while the client orchestrator is the top-level dashboard that surfaces metrics, the inbox, approvals, and the agent roster. This is the human cockpit for the company-agent system — the surface where autonomous work becomes visible and approvable.

tour.title: Agent Drawer & Streaming Chat Endpoint
tour.description: The CEO and directors are not just background workers — an admin can chat with them directly. The agent drawer is the slide-out chat shell, and the company-agent message endpoint streams a CEO-orchestrator turn over Server-Sent Events. This connects the dashboard UI from Step 8 to the orchestration brain you are about to meet.
tour.languageLesson: Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream tokens one-way from server to browser over a long-lived HTTP response. Next.js route handlers return a streaming Response whose body is an async generator of `data:` frames — ideal for live LLM output.

tour.title: The Agent Hierarchy: CEO, Directors & EA
tour.description: This is the heart of the autonomous system. The CEO orchestrator assembles company context and metrics and delegates to directors; the shared company-agent runner is the core runtime that loads memory, conversation history, and skills for any agent; and the marketing director and executive assistant are thin role entry points that run through that shared runner. Together they form a delegating hierarchy modeled on a real company org chart.

tour.title: Skills, Action Executors & the Audit Trail
tour.description: Agents act through skills and actions. The skills registry (the highest fan-out file in the project) aggregates every role-specific capability the runner can invoke. Proposed actions flow through shared action domain logic with Zod payload schemas, and the action-executor registry turns approved actions into real side effects. The audit utilities wrap every agent call so the dashboard can replay exactly what happened.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas validate untrusted payloads at runtime and infer their TypeScript types at compile time — one source of truth for both. Per-action schemas here guarantee an LLM-proposed action is well-formed before it can ever be executed.

tour.title: Guardrails, Spend Caps & Shared Integrations
tour.description: Autonomy without limits is dangerous, so guardrails define risk tiers that decide whether an action auto-executes or requires human approval, and the spend module enforces a monthly token-cost cap that can pause the whole fleet. These lean on shared integrations: the Anthropic client factory and the Supabase-backed sliding-window rate limiter, both high-fan-in utilities used across customer and company agents alike.

tour.title: Autonomous Runs: Heartbeats & Cron Infrastructure
tour.description: The capstone ties the system together over time. The heartbeats module computes each agent's schedule and the next fire time, the dynamic cron route wakes a given company-agent role on a tick, and the execute-approved-actions cron picks up approved actions and dispatches them to their executors. The GitHub Actions workflow pings that executor cron on a schedule, making the whole Command Center run on its own. This is how the org chart from Step 10 becomes genuinely autonomous.
tour.languageLesson: YAML cron workflows in GitHub Actions use an `on.schedule` trigger with standard cron syntax. Here it simply pings an HTTP endpoint on an interval — a lightweight, externally-driven heartbeat that complements Vercel's own scheduled cron jobs from Step 2.
